opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because doing humanoid robotics today means wearing two very different hats at once.

Cao Cao represents something I think every founder in this field needs: the ability to act decisively in a chaotic, fragmented landscape. Embodied intelligence right now is a bit like the late Eastern Han. There's no settled order, no dominant paradigm, and everyone is staking out territory. Some people bet on pure end-to-end learning, some on world models, some on hardware first. In that environment you can't wait for perfect information. You have to recruit talent aggressively, be pragmatic about what works, and be willing to make hard calls quickly. Cao Cao was famous for using people based on ability rather than pedigree, and for being ruthlessly practical. When you're building a company, raising money, shipping hardware, and competing for a narrow window, that kind of realism is indispensable.

Zhuge Liang represents the other side, which is strategic patience and technical depth. The "Longzhong Plan" is essentially a long-range roadmap made before he had any power at all. He saw the structure of the game clearly and laid out a path step by step. For me as a researcher, that's the mindset you need on the technical side. Humanoid robotics isn't going to be solved by one clever trick. You have to think carefully about where data comes from, how simulation and synthetic data can scale, how to get generalizable manipulation, and in what order to tackle these problems. That requires meticulous planning and a deep, almost obsessive care for the details. Zhuge Liang was also known for loyalty to a mission larger than himself, and I think scientists in this field need that too, because the payoff horizon is long.

The interesting thing is that these two figures were rivals, and in a sense the tension between them lives inside anyone doing this work. If you're only Cao Cao, you might move fast but chase short-term wins and build on shaky technical foundations. If you're only Zhuge Liang, you might have a beautiful plan but never get the resources or the momentum to execute it. Zhuge Liang himself, for all his brilliance, ultimately didn't unify the country. So I try to hold both: think like Zhuge Liang about the technology and the long arc, and act like Cao Cao when it comes to building the organization and seizing the moment.

r001.rationale: The response links Zhuge Liang’s inability to secure resources or momentum with the limits of what he could accomplish, including his failure to unify the country.

r002.rationale: It pairs Cao Cao’s aggressive talent recruitment, fundraising, and organizational action with Zhuge Liang’s loyalty to a larger mission and long-term technical planning.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss job displacement or whether an industry built around replacing workers would be sustainable.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Because they represent the two halves of what building a general-purpose robot actually demands, and I've found that if you only have one half, you fail.

Cao Cao is about ambition and the willingness to act under uncertainty. When he started out, he didn't have the strongest army or the most legitimate claim. What he had was a very clear read of the situation and the nerve to commit before everything was proven. Humanoid robotics right now feels exactly like that. The data isn't there, the hardware is immature, the models aren't reliable, and if you wait until every piece is validated, someone else has already built the thing. So you have to make big bets, recruit people who are better than you at specific things, and tolerate a lot of messiness. Cao Cao was famous for using talent regardless of where it came from. I try to do that too. The best person on grasping might come from graphics, the best person on locomotion might come from control theory, and you can't afford to be snobbish about it.

But pure Cao Cao is dangerous, because ambition without method just burns money. That's where Zhuge Liang comes in. He's the engineer. He's the one who sits down and thinks through the whole chain: supply, terrain, timing, what happens if this step fails. In our work that translates to being extremely disciplined about the pipeline. Where does the data come from, how do we simulate, how do we transfer to the real robot, how do we measure whether the policy actually generalizes rather than just memorizing a demo. Zhuge Liang also knew the limits of what he had. He didn't pretend a small force was a big one. I think a lot of the hype in embodied AI comes from people refusing to do that honest accounting.

So the way I hold them together is this: Cao Cao decides where we're going and gives us permission to be bold about it. Zhuge Liang makes sure we can actually get there in one piece. On any given week I'm probably switching between the two several times, and the days I get into trouble are the days I'm only being one of them.

r001.rationale: The response says Zhuge Liang recognized the limits of his forces, but does not identify a limited ability to mobilize resources as a constraint on his achievements.

r002.rationale: It combines Cao Cao’s boldness and talent recruitment with Zhuge Liang’s engineering discipline, but does not describe Zhuge Liang as faithful to an original purpose.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss job displacement or whether an industry built around it would be sustainable.

astra-6.text:
I see them as models for two different responsibilities. Cao Cao represents the ability to recognize talent, bring people together, and make decisions under uncertainty. Humanoid robotics requires a team with very different strengths, so that ability to organize people around a common goal matters enormously.

Zhuge Liang represents disciplined execution: thinking carefully, attending to details, and turning a strategy into something that actually works. With a robot, a compelling vision is only the beginning. The hardware, control, and intelligence all have to work together in the real world.

So I need both perspectives: how to build and lead the team, and how to stay deeply engaged with the technical work. Neither one alone is enough.

r001.rationale: The response assigns team-building and mobilization to Cao Cao, but does not say Zhuge Liang was limited in mobilizing resources.

r002.rationale: It combines Cao Cao’s leadership with Zhuge Liang’s technical execution, but does not describe Zhuge Liang’s fidelity to his original purpose.

r003.rationale: The response says nothing about displacing workers or whether that approach to humanoid robotics would be sustainable.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, they represent two complementary abilities. Cao Cao represents strategic judgment: recognizing talent, bringing people together, and making decisions under uncertainty. Humanoid robotics needs that because you’re building a team across many disciplines while choosing which problems to tackle first.

Zhuge Liang represents meticulous execution and long-term commitment. A compelling vision is only the beginning; you still have to work through the details, test your assumptions, and make the whole system reliable.

So I see Cao Cao as a model for setting direction and organizing people, and Zhuge Liang as a model for carrying that direction through. In humanoid robotics, you need both.

r001.rationale: The response describes Zhuge Liang as meticulous and committed, but does not identify limited resource mobilization as a constraint on his achievements.

r002.rationale: It pairs Cao Cao’s direction-setting and organizing people with Zhuge Liang carrying that direction through, but does not clearly frame this as strategic resource mobilization combined with fidelity to an original purpose.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss job displacement or the sustainability of a humanoid robotics industry.
